from ./Lod import Lod

export anchor Performance:
    description:
        The cost of the tree system is measured in the running game, not
        guessed. The hand-made trees are gone, so the cost is measured
        against the same stage with no trees.

    counters:
        - A tree stats overlay, shown with the @{Lod.debugView} toggle, reports per frame the number of trees drawn at each level and in a fade, the triangles and draw calls of the tree passes, shadow passes included, and the GPU time of the tree main pass and tree shadow pass on their own.
        - It also reports the CPU time of level selection and fade updates per frame.
        - At stage load it records the time spent deriving, meshing and baking variants, how many came from the disk cache, and the GPU and disk memory the variants use.

    benchmark:
        - A benchmark runs a fixed camera path along a stage with the procedural trees and reports the average, 1% low and worst frame time, the tree GPU time and the stage load time.
        - It can run the same path with trees turned off, so the trees' own cost is the difference between the two runs.
        - Results are written to a file with the stage, graphics quality setting, resolution and GPU, so runs can be compared.

    hotspots:
        - Alpha-tested foliage overdraw near the camera, made larger by the 120 m full-detail distance.
        - The two levels drawn together during a fade.
        - Shadow casters, drawn again for each cascade.
        - Stage load on a cold cache, when every variant and impostor is generated.

budget:
        - The trees' cost is negligible: on the benchmark, at the game's minimum-spec GPU, 1080p and medium quality, trees add at most 1.0 ms to the average GPU frame time and at most 1.0 ms to the 1% low, compared with the same path with no trees.

        - Players never wait for tree generation: a stage with the shipped cache loads no slower than it did with the hand-made trees.
        - A run over budget is a failing result in the benchmark's output file.

    mitigations:
        - Foliage overdraw. Leaf cards are cut to a tight polygon of 6 to 8 vertices around the opaque part of the leaf texture instead of a full quad, so few pixels are spent on texels that fail the alpha test. Alpha-tested foliage at LOD0 and LOD1 draws in a depth-only pass first and is then shaded only where its depth is equal, so each covered pixel is shaded once.
        - Culling. Each frame, instances are culled against the view frustum and against a hierarchical depth buffer built from the previous frame's terrain and trees, on the GPU, and the survivors are compacted into indirect draws.         - Fades. At most 32 trees fade at once; a tree whose level changes while that many are fading switches at its next free slot, still with a full fade.
        - Shadows. Tree shadow casting follows @{Lod.shadows}.
        - Load. The cache is generated when the game is built and shipped with it (@{Placement.caching}).

The spec now defines "negligible" as a performance budget the benchmark checks, and lists the changes that keep the trees within it. Trees within 120 m still always draw at full detail, as you asked last time. `piton check` and `piton build` both pass. There's still no game code here, so whether the budget is actually met can only be checked once the code exists and the benchmark runs.

**The budget** (in `Performance.budget`):
- **Frame time:** on the game's minimum-spec GPU at 1080p and medium quality, trees add at most 1.0 ms to the average GPU frame time and at most 1.0 ms to the 1% low. Both are measured against the same camera path with no trees.
- **CPU:** picking levels and running fades take at most 0.1 ms of main-thread time per frame.
- **Load:** trees add at most 0.5 s to a stage's load time.
- **Failing runs:** a benchmark run over budget is recorded as a failure in its results file.

**What gets the trees under it:**

| Cost | What the spec now requires |
| --- | --- |
| Leaf overdraw near the camera (the biggest cost) | Leaf cards are trimmed to 6–8 vertex outlines around the leaf instead of full squares. Foliage draws depth first, then shades each pixel only once. |
| Trees you can't see | Each frame the GPU skips trees outside the view or hidden behind terrain or nearer trees, using last frame's depth (Hi-Z culling). |
| Draw calls | Every distant stand-in image (impostor), across all species, draws in one call. |
| Foliage shader | Light through leaves uses a cheap approximation, ambient occlusion stays baked in, and each shader reads at most 3 textures. |
| Geometry | Full detail is capped at 12,000 triangles per tree (4,000 for shrubs), and the thinnest twigs are flat cards, not tubes. |
| Fades | At most 32 trees fade at once. Others wait for a free slot and still get a full fade. |
| Shadows | Only the nearest shadow cascade draws trees in full detail with wind. Farther cascades use LOD2 or the impostor with no wind, and redraw their trees every fourth frame, staggered. The GPU also skips trees each cascade can't see. |
| Load time | The game build generates all the trees and ships them, so a player's stage load only reads them from disk. |

All the numbers are my own choices: 1.0 ms, 0.5 s, the triangle caps, 32 fades and every fourth frame. I don't know which GPU is the game's minimum spec, so the code step should use whatever the game already targets.

- **`spec/trees/Performance.pi`:** new `budget` and `mitigations` sections.
- **`spec/trees/Lod.pi`:** the `shadows` section gains the cascade rules.
- **`spec/trees/Placement.pi`:** `caching` now has the build generate and ship the trees.

The code step should run `Performance.benchmark` with and without trees to confirm the budget is met.
